Lodgepole vs Ponderosa

How to tell the two pines apart at the tree. Facts from the Colorado State Forest Service.

The 5-second test: pull one needle bundle and count

2 short needles (1–3 in, often twisted) = lodgepole.

3 long needles (3–7 in) = ponderosa.

Then check the bark: big orange plates on a mature trunk means ponderosa; thin, light brown, small scales means lodgepole.

Lodgepole pine Pinus contorta

Ponderosa pine Pinus ponderosa

LodgepolePonderosa
Needles per bundle23 (typically)
Needle length1–3 in, stiff, sharp, often twisted3–7 in, in tufts near the branch ends
BarkThin, light brown, many small scalesMature: red-orange, thick, big flat plates. Young trees: dark
ConesUp to 2 in, shiny yellow-brown; often stay closed on the branch (open with heat)3–4 in, light red-brown, each scale ends in a sharp point
Height20–80 ft40–160 ft
How they growOften in pure, crowded standsOpen, park-like stands
Elevation6,000–11,000 ft6,300–9,500 ft

Bailey sits inside both trees' elevation ranges, so expect either, or both on one lot. Ponderosa is the bigger tree (up to 160 ft against lodgepole's 80), which matters for the felling price.

Source: Colorado State Forest Service, Colorado's Major Tree Species (read 11 Oct 2026).
